title: Design Top-K trending
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, sliding windows, Count-Min Sketch, heavy hitters, stream aggregation.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Top-K trending finds the K most popular items (hashtags, searches, videos, products) in a recent time window, for example "top 10 hashtags in the last hour". Twitter/X trends, YouTube trending, Google Trends, and "trending searches" in an e-commerce app are examples. The difficulty is counting a firehose of events without storing or sorting all of them.

Functional requirements

  • Ingest a stream of events (a hashtag was used, a video was viewed).
  • Return the top K items for a window: last 1 minute, 1 hour, 24 hours.
  • Optionally per region or per category.
  • Trending means a surge, not just the biggest all-time count.

Non-functional requirements

  • Freshness: results within 1-5 s for the minute window, within a minute for longer windows.
  • Query latency under 20 ms (served from a precomputed result).
  • Scale: 1M events/s peak, 100M distinct items.
  • Approximate answers are acceptable (the 10th item being off by 0.5% does not matter); the system must never fall over.

Decision gravity. Choose approximate counting (Count-Min Sketch plus a heap, or sampling) over exact counts in a database, because exact per-item counters for 100M items across 1M events/s are expensive and unnecessary. Reversible: you can later run an exact batch job in parallel to correct the approximation (the Lambda-style pattern).

Everyday analogy. A radio station's weekly chart: they do not track every listener; a sample is enough to rank the songs.

Common interview traps.

  • Using SELECT item, COUNT(*) GROUP BY item ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10 on raw events.
  • Forgetting the time window (counts of "all time" are not trending).
  • Treating trending as just "most frequent", ignoring burst/velocity.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
GET /v1/trending?scope=global&window=1h&k=10
200 { "window": "1h", "computedAt": "2026-11-09T14:00:05Z",
      "items": [ { "rank":1, "item":"#worldcup", "count": 1843221, "delta": "+380%" },
                 { "rank":2, "item":"#elections", "count": 1520014, "delta": "+25%" } ] }
GET /v1/trending?scope=region:IN&window=5m&k=20&category=sports
200 { ... }
POST /v1/events                 // internal, batched
{ "events": [ { "item":"#worldcup", "region":"IN", "ts": 1731160800123, "weight": 1 },
              { "item":"#worldcup", "region":"US", "ts": 1731160800150, "weight": 1 } ] }
202 Accepted

Events are sent by producers (app servers, clients through a collector) in batches of 100-1000 to cut overhead; weight lets a retweet count more than a view. The read API is cacheable: Cache-Control: public, max-age=5.

Industry examples. Twitter's trends API and Google Trends expose a window + geo dimension; YouTube's trending tab is refreshed periodically, not per second.

Everyday analogy. A newsstand's "best sellers this week" sign, updated once in a while rather than after each sale.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering one endpoint per window as separate code paths instead of one parameterised query.
  • No region/category dimension.
  • Making the read API compute rankings on demand.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 1M events/s peak (about 300k/s average), 100M distinct items per day, K = 100.

Quantity Calculation Result
Event size item id 16 B + region 2 B + ts 8 B + overhead ~50 B
Ingest bandwidth 1M x 50 B 50 MB/s
Raw event storage 300k/s x 86,400 x 50 B ~1.3 TB/day (keep a few days in Kafka/S3)
Exact counters 100M items x (16 B key + 8 B count) ~2.4 GB per window: fits in RAM, but update rate is high
Windows 1 min, 1 h, 24 h; per region (200) exact map per (window x region) explodes: ~600 maps
Count-Min Sketch width 2^20 x depth 4 x 4 B counters 16 MB per sketch, error under 0.0001 x total events
Kafka partitions 1M msgs/s; a partition handles ~50-100k msgs/s 20-30 partitions
Final result K=100 items x 50 B 5 KB per (scope, window): trivial

The input rate is the issue, not the output. Heavy hitters are few; the bulk of the 100M items appear once or twice and do not matter.

Industry example. Twitter/X reported processing hundreds of thousands of tweets per second at peak; trends are computed from streams (Storm/Heron lineage) with sketches.

Everyday analogy. Counting the crowd's cheers for each team with a few tally sheets, not an individual list for every spectator.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating only the final answer's size.
  • Using one hot Redis key for a counter at 1M/s.
  • Not computing sketch sizes.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • Kafka: events partitioned by hash(item) so all events for one item land on one worker; no cross-worker double counting.
  • Stream workers (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming): each keeps a local Count-Min Sketch or exact map per window, and a min-heap of its local top K.
  • Aggregator: merges local heaps from all workers into the global top K every 1-5 s (since items are partitioned by hash, global top K is the top K of the union of local top K lists).
  • Top-K cache: Redis keys such as trend:global:1h storing a small JSON/ZSET, TTL 60 s.
  • Batch layer (optional): hourly Spark job computes exact counts from the raw log in S3 and corrects the speed layer.
  • Trending API: stateless, reads Redis, adds metadata (names, thumbnails).

Decision gravity: partition by item, merge local top-K. Why: because each item lives on exactly one worker, local counts are exact (no merging counters) and merging K-lists is cheap. Alternative: partition by event round-robin and merge sketches (sketches add cell by cell), which balances load for hot items but needs more memory per worker and a bigger merge. Breaks with one mega hot item (a single partition gets 10% of traffic): split hot keys into sub-keys with random suffixes and sum later. Reversible by reprocessing from Kafka.

Decision gravity: stream vs batch. Stream processing gives seconds of freshness. Batch-only (hourly MapReduce) is simple and exact but stale. Lambda architecture runs both: fast approximate now, corrected later. Kappa architecture uses only the stream with replay. Choose Kappa unless you need exact audited counts.

Industry examples. Twitter's trends pipeline, LinkedIn's trending, Netflix's Top 10 (batch daily), Uber's surge uses windows.

Everyday analogy. Each cashier keeps a tally of her own best sellers; the manager only compares the cashiers' short lists.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing the global top K by sorting all counters.
  • Forgetting that top K of a union needs each worker's top K (not just top 1).
  • No answer for a single dominating hot key.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Counting windows

A sliding window of 1 hour is built from 60 one-minute buckets. Every minute: add the newest bucket, subtract (drop) the oldest. Store counts per (item, minuteBucket). For the 24 h window use 24 one-hour buckets (rolled up from minute buckets). Memory = items x buckets, so only track candidate heavy hitters rather than all 100M items. Tumbling windows (fixed, non-overlapping) are cheaper but show jumps at boundaries; Flink supports sliding windows natively.

Count-Min Sketch

A 2-D array of d rows by w columns of counters. To add an item, hash it with d hash functions and increment one cell per row. To estimate, take the minimum of its d cells (collisions only overestimate). Error: estimate <= true + epsilon x N with probability 1 - delta, where w = e/epsilon and d = ln(1/delta). With w = 2^20 and d = 4 the error is about 3 x 10^-6 x N; at N = 3.6 billion events/hour that is about 10,000 extra, negligible for items with millions of hits.

import heapq, mmh3   # mmh3 = MurmurHash3
class CMS:
    def __init__(self, w=1<<20, d=4):
        self.w, self.d = w, d
        self.t = [[0]*w for _ in range(d)]
    def add(self, x, c=1):
        for i in range(self.d):
            self.t[i][mmh3.hash(x, i) % self.w] += c
    def est(self, x):
        return min(self.t[i][mmh3.hash(x, i) % self.w] for i in range(self.d))

The sketch cannot list its keys, so pair it with a min-heap of size K: after each add, if the item's estimate beats the heap's smallest, insert it. Alternative: the Space-Saving algorithm keeps exactly m counters (for example 10,000) and evicts the smallest, giving guaranteed heavy-hitter detection with tiny memory. Decision gravity: sketch vs exact map: pick the sketch when memory per window matters and ranks need not be perfect; reversible by switching the worker implementation.

Trending is velocity, not volume

"Top by count" shows always-popular items (#love). To detect a surge, compare the current window to a baseline: score = (current - expected) / sqrt(expected + 1) (z-score style) or ratio current / avg of same hour over last 7 days. Twitter described novelty as part of trends. Keep a slow baseline sketch per item for the long window and a fast one for the recent window; the difference ranks "rising" items. Filter spam and blocklisted topics before publishing.

Merging and the hot key

When one item gets a huge share, salt its key into n sub-keys (#worldcup#7), count independently, then sum in the aggregator. Detect hot keys by sampling 1% of events.

Publishing results

Aggregator pushes the merged top K to Redis every 1-5 s as an atomic RENAME of a temp key (readers never see half a list). Add a "last good" fallback if the pipeline stalls. CDN-cache the API for 5 s so 100k user reads/s become a handful of origin hits.

Fault tolerance and exactly-once

Flink checkpoints state (sketches, heaps) to S3 every minute with Kafka offsets; on crash it restarts from the checkpoint and reprocesses: counts are consistent (exactly-once state semantics). Late events beyond the watermark (say 30 s) are dropped or sent to a correction batch. Replaying Kafka allows recomputation after a bug fix. Decision: event time vs processing time; event time with watermarks is correct for mobile clients that send late.

Dimensions: region and category

Add region/category to the key: (region, item). Number of sketches = windows x regions. Compute global as the sum of regional sketches (sketches add cell-wise) instead of counting twice. Keep top-K per region only for the top 50 regions; the rest roll up.

Production incident patterns. (1) A single partition lagging because of a hot key: Kafka consumer lag on one partition; mitigate with key salting. (2) Trending list stuck for 10 minutes because the aggregator died: monitor computedAt age and alert at 30 s. (3) Spam campaigns hijacking trends: add distinct-user counting (HyperLogLog, 12 KB per item) so 10,000 posts from 5 accounts do not outrank 5,000 posts from 5,000 accounts.

Industry examples. Twitter/X trends, YouTube trending, Google Trends, Redis HyperLogLog (PFADD) for distinct users.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer counting how many different people walk in, not just how many times one person walks through the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Count-Min Sketch with no heap, so you cannot list items.
  • Using processing time and getting wrong windows for late mobile events.
  • Equating trending with raw popularity.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Recognising this as streaming heavy-hitters, not a SQL group-by.
  • Sliding windows built from buckets, and the memory trade-off.
  • Count-Min Sketch or Space-Saving with a heap, with error reasoning.
  • Merging local top-K lists after partitioning by item; hot-key salting.
  • Distinguishing velocity from volume, and spam resistance (distinct users via HyperLogLog).
  • Operational view: checkpoints, replay, freshness metric, cached read API.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Stream events into Kafka partitioned by item; workers keep windowed counts and local top-K heaps.
  • A global aggregator merges the local lists every few seconds and writes a small result to Redis.
  • Sliding windows are sums of small time buckets; trending uses growth relative to a baseline.
  • Count-Min Sketch (16 MB) plus a min-heap, or Space-Saving, gives bounded error with tiny memory.
  • Salt hot keys; use HyperLogLog for distinct users to resist spam.
  • Checkpoint state and replay from Kafka for recovery; optionally correct with an hourly exact batch.
  • The API only reads a precomputed, CDN-cacheable result.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Count-Min Sketch count items, why does it take the minimum of its cells, and why can it only overestimate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Top-K at 1M events/s needs approximate counting; the signal is whether you understand the error direction and the memory trade.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It is a 2-D array of d rows by w columns of counters. To add an item I hash it with d different hash functions and increment one cell per row. To estimate, I read its d cells and take the minimum. Collisions with other items only add to a cell, never subtract, so every cell is at least the true count and the minimum is the least-polluted one. The estimate is at most true + epsilon * N with probability 1 - delta, where w = e/epsilon and d = ln(1/delta).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
add("#wc"):   row0[h0 % w]++   row1[h1 % w]++   row2[h2 % w]++   row3[h3 % w]++
est("#wc") =  min(row0[h0 % w], row1[h1 % w], row2[h2 % w], row3[h3 % w])

With w = 2^20 and d = 4, a sketch is 2^20 x 4 x 4 B = 16 MB. Epsilon is about 2.6e-6. At N = 3.6 billion events per hour the worst-case extra is about 9,400, negligible for items with millions of hits but fatal for items with hundreds. The sketch cannot list its keys, so it must be paired with a min-heap of size K (or Space-Saving).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CMS:
    def __init__(self, w=1 << 20, d=4):
        self.w, self.d = w, d
        self.t = [[0] * w for _ in range(d)]
    def add(self, x, c=1):
        for i in range(self.d):
            self.t[i][hash((i, x)) % self.w] += c
    def est(self, x):
        return min(self.t[i][hash((i, x)) % self.w] for i in range(self.d))

(Use a stable hash such as MurmurHash3 in production; Python's hash of strings changes per process.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the sketch can return the list of heavy items.
  • Using it for low-count items where error exceeds the count.
  • Using non-independent hash functions for the rows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can sketches be merged? -> Yes, add cell by cell, if shapes and hash seeds match.
  2. Can you delete or expire? -> Not directly; use per-bucket sketches and drop old ones.
  3. Sketch versus Space-Saving? -> Space-Saving keeps m exact-ish counters and guarantees heavy hitters; the sketch is simpler to merge.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "approximate counter". Senior: error bound formula, memory sizing, heap pairing, mergeability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams tune width after seeing top-K tails full of noise when traffic grows 10x and N inflates the error.

questions.promptHtml: "#love" has the highest count every hour. Why is it not trending, and how do you rank what is trending?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates stop at heavy hitters; trending is about velocity against a baseline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Trending means a surge relative to normal, not the biggest count. I keep a fast window count and a slow baseline per item, and rank by how far the current window exceeds expectation, for example (current - expected) / sqrt(expected + 1) or a ratio against the same hour over the last 7 days. Always-popular items have high expected values so they score low. I also filter spam and blocklisted topics before publishing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
item     current(1h)  expected    score = (cur-exp)/sqrt(exp+1)
#love       500,000     480,000     ~29
#worldcup 1,800,000      40,000    ~8,800

Keep the 1-minute and 1-hour windows from buckets, and a slow baseline (7-day same hour-of-week) in a separate sketch. Smooth to avoid noise for tiny counts: the +1 and a minimum-volume threshold. New items have no baseline; use a prior (global average) so a brand new tag with 50 events does not top the list.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ranking by raw count.
  • No minimum volume, so rare tags with 3 events versus 0 baseline rank first.
  • Ignoring that baseline depends on hour of week.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you prevent flicker? -> Smooth scores over several windows and keep a hysteresis band before swapping rank positions.
  2. Where does the baseline live? -> A slow sketch or a daily batch job writing per-item expected counts.
  3. How do you handle holidays? -> Same hour-of-week misses events; add year-over-year seasonality or accept it and label.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: top by count. Senior: statistical surge score, baseline sketch, minimum volume, and spam filtering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A trends product showing only evergreen tags had near-zero engagement until velocity ranking replaced raw counts.

questions.contextHtml: Today: 1M events/s peak, sketch per (window, region) of w=2^20, d=4 (16 MB). The product now wants 10M events/s, 200 regions, windows of 1 min, 1 h and 24 h. A reviewer says "the error bound will eat our top 100". Current hourly global N is 3.6 billion; the 100th item has about 400,000 hits in the hour.
questions.promptHtml: Does the sketch still work at 10x, and what is the sizing and architecture change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps the same sketch, or switches to exact counters for 100M items without math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is top-100 global only, or per region too? What error is acceptable in the 100th position? Distribution across regions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; do the math first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Error scales with N: epsilon = e/2^20 = 2.6e-6; at N = 36 billion per hour the extra is up to about 94,000. The 100th item at 400,000 hits (10x it becomes 4M) tolerates that error (2.3 percent), so global top-100 is still fine. Regional sketches have much smaller N, so error is small there.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the new production-shaped stream against the sketch plus an exact offline count for a day; compare rank overlap of top-100.
  5. Root cause: Not an incident; error is proportional to total volume N.
  6. Fix: Keep w = 2^20 for regions; widen the global hourly sketch to 2^22 (64 MB with d=4) if needed. Memory: 600 sketches x 16 MB is under 10 GB spread across workers, fine. Ingest: 10M x 50 B = 500 MB/s, about 200 Kafka partitions at 50k/s each. Local top-K heaps per worker plus aggregator merge stay unchanged.
  7. Prevention: Track rank overlap against a sampled exact count; alert when the heap's K-th estimate approaches epsilon * N.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not move to exact maps for 100M items per window; I would not shrink K or lengthen windows to hide the error.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if they want top-10 per minute per region? -> N per minute per region is tiny; use Space-Saving with 10k counters.
  • What if one event type dominates (80 percent)? -> Sample or split by type to keep N small per sketch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A trending list degraded after a global event tripled traffic: the sketch had not changed, N had, and the tail of top-100 filled with noise.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: No error math.
  • Hire: Computes epsilon x N and compares to the K-th count.
  • Strong hire: Regional/global split, validation against exact sample, partition and bandwidth math.

questions.contextHtml:
During a cup final, trending freshness jumps from 3 s to 4 minutes. Kafka consumer lag is high on exactly one of 32 partitions; the other 31 are at zero lag. Worker CPU for that partition's consumer is at 100 percent and its heap is 90 percent full.

group trend-workers  partition 17  lag 18,400,000
group trend-workers  partition 0..16,18..31  lag 0

Topic is keyed by hash(item); #cupfinal is getting 12 percent of all events.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without restarting the pipeline from scratch.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add partitions" (the hot key still maps to one partition).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the skew one key or a range? Are events for the item order-sensitive? Is the aggregator reading local top-K lists?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Salt the key: producers append a random suffix 0-9 for items flagged hot, spreading #cupfinal over 10 partitions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a single hot item; (b) a bad deploy slowing one worker; (c) a poison message; (d) a rebalance. Lag on only one partition with a hot key points at (a).
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample 1 percent of events by key to find the top keys; compare consumer CPU per instance; check for rebalance events in the group log.
  5. Root cause: Partitioning by item guarantees all events of one item reach one worker; one item at 12 percent of 1M/s is 120k/s, above a single consumer's capacity.
  6. Fix: Salt hot keys into n sub-keys, count independently, and sum in the aggregator. Add a hot-key detector (sampling) that updates the salt list dynamically. Replay the backlog from the lagging partition after salting.
  7. Prevention: Per-partition lag alerts, hot-key detection, load tests with a Zipf distribution.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add partitions alone and I would not drop events silently. Salting loses the "exact, single-owner" property: the aggregator must sum sub-key counts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not partition round-robin and merge sketches? -> Balances hot items but needs bigger per-worker memory and merge cost.
  • Local top-K lists: any issue after salting? -> The hot item may not appear in every worker's top K; sum sub-key counts before ranking.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single celebrity hashtag lagged one partition for 40 minutes; the dashboard showed average lag across partitions, which was fine, so nothing paged.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds partitions or scales consumers.
  • Hire: Identifies the hot key and salts it.
  • Strong hire: Dynamic hot-key detection, correct merge after salting, per-partition lag alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report the trending list is "stuck" on yesterday's evening topics. The API is healthy (p99 8 ms) and returns 200. The aggregator pod was OOM-killed 40 minutes ago and its replacement is crash-looping on startup. Redis shows:

GET trend:global:1h   -> {"computedAt":"2026-11-09T13:20:04Z", ...}
TTL trend:global:1h   -> -1

Stream workers and Kafka are fine.
questions.promptHtml: Why did nothing alert, and how do you harden publishing?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restarts the aggregator and moves on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the freshness SLO? Is "last good" acceptable for how long? Why is the aggregator OOMing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart with more memory; check why it crashes (the merge of local top-K lists should be tiny; maybe it loads full sketches).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) aggregator regression holding all local counts; (b) huge heap messages after a hot item; (c) a bad deploy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pod events and heap dump, message sizes into the aggregator, deploy history.
  5. Root cause: The result key has no TTL and the API never checks computedAt age, so a dead aggregator is invisible: the API serves a valid but stale list forever.
  6. Fix: Publish with an atomic RENAME of a temp key; add computedAt to the payload and alert when now - computedAt > 30 s; API returns a header X-Stale: true or falls back to a longer window when beyond a limit; run two aggregator replicas (leader election or idempotent writes).
  7. Prevention: Freshness SLI on the output, synthetic canary read, chaos test killing the aggregator.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set a short TTL that empties the page at the first hiccup; stale-but-labelled beats blank for a trends list.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why RENAME? -> Readers see either the old or the new complete list, never a half-written one.
  • Two aggregators writing? -> Same inputs give the same list; last-write-wins with computedAt monotonic check.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "trending now" tab showed the previous night's topics all morning because every health check looked at the API, not at the age of the data.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Restarts and closes.
  • Hire: Adds data-age metric and atomic publish.
  • Strong hire: Replicated aggregator, stale labelling, synthetic canary, rationale for no hard TTL.

questions.contextHtml: A political hashtag #vote2026xyz is rank 1 in trending, with 480,000 posts in an hour. Moderators say 94 percent of its posts come from about 600 accounts. Meanwhile #rainstorm has 210,000 posts from 190,000 distinct accounts and is rank 6. Users complain the trends are being gamed. Each item currently has a sketch count only.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign counting so a coordinated burst does not dominate, within memory and latency limits.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blocklists and manual review only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are accounts authenticated, and can we trust account IDs? What counts as one vote per window per user? Is blocking coordinated behaviour in scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Manual demotion of the item, rate-limit per user per item (cap at 1 to 3 counts per hour).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Bot ring; a legit but narrow community; a retweet storm. Distinguish by distinct-account ratio.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute distinct users per item for the window: 600 vs 190,000.
  5. Root cause: The score counts events, not people.
  6. Fix: Add a HyperLogLog per candidate item (about 12 KB, error around 1 percent; Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT, or in-process HLL in workers) for distinct users; rank by a score that uses distinct users (for example sqrt(events) * distinctUsers or distinct users alone), and enforce per-user caps. Apply HLL only to heap candidates (top few thousand), not to 100M items. HLLs are mergeable, so they fit the local-to-global merge.
  7. Prevention: Account age/reputation weighting, anomaly detection on distinct ratio, review queue for entries that enter top 10.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: HLL cannot say who the users are; I would keep a small sampled exact set for investigations. I would not rank purely by distinct users if that suppresses legitimate fast-growing tags with few users.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory for 5,000 candidates? -> 5,000 x 12 KB = 60 MB per window per worker; fine.
  • What about sybil accounts (50,000 fresh bots)? -> Add account-age and device signals; distinct counting alone is insufficient.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campaign pushed a tag to number one from 400 accounts for two hours; distinct-user counting would have placed it near rank 300.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blocklists only.
  • Hire: Distinct-user counting with HLL.
  • Strong hire: HLL on candidates only, mergeability, per-user caps, sybil limits.

questions.contextHtml: The ads team wants the trending feed to also drive a paid "sponsored trend" product with invoices, so they ask for "exact" counts for the last hour and an audit trail. Mobile clients upload events up to 10 minutes late when offline. The current system is streaming (Kafka, Flink) with sketches and a 30 s watermark; late events are dropped.
questions.promptHtml: What do you propose: pure stream, Lambda or Kappa, and how do you handle late data?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switches everything to exact counts in a database, or says "approximate is fine" without asking about billing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is exactness for the public ranking or only for billing? What error is invoiced against? How late can data be and is it replayed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; separate the two needs: ranking tolerates approximation, billing must be exact and reproducible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The public list stays approximate; billing needs a separate exact path.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare batch exact counts with the stream's for a week; measure how many events arrive after the watermark.
  5. Root cause: One system is trying to serve two correctness contracts.
  6. Fix: Keep the stream (Kappa) for the public list. Add a batch layer that recomputes exact counts hourly from raw events in object storage (Spark), by event time, including late arrivals; billing reads only from that. Raise the watermark to a few minutes for the public path or send late events to a correction topic; accept that the public list will not include them until the batch result. Flink checkpoints (state plus Kafka offsets) every minute give exactly-once state; the raw log gives audit.
  7. Prevention: Daily reconciliation between stream and batch, with an alert on divergence beyond tolerance.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the real-time path exact: it would cost far more memory and latency for a list where 0.5 percent error is invisible. Lambda doubles code paths; accept it only for the billing slice.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not event time everywhere? -> Event time with watermarks is right for ranking; for billing you can wait for the batch.
  • Late events after batch closes? -> Billing cut-off rule (for example T+24 h) in the contract.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A metrics number was billed from a streaming job; a replay after a bug fix changed totals and the finance team lost a week reconciling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Exactness everywhere, or ignores billing.
  • Hire: Separates ranking from billing with a batch layer.
  • Strong hire: Watermark policy, reconciliation, audit trail, and cost argument.

questions.contextHtml:
A worker keeps a sketch and a "top K" heap. In production the top-10 is often a single item repeated, and old items never leave. Review:

K = 10
cms = CMS()
heap = []                    # (estimate, item)

def on_event(item):
    cms.add(item)
    est = cms.est(item)
    if len(heap) < K or est > heap[0][0]:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (est, item))
        if len(heap) > K:
            heapq.heappop(heap)

def top():
    return sorted(heap, reverse=True)

Traffic: #worldcup gets 100k events/s.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and give a correct design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only notices style issues; misses that the heap holds duplicates.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is this per window? Is it single-threaded? Does time ever pass in this structure?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rebuild top() from the sketch's candidate set rather than trusting the heap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the same item is pushed repeatedly with increasing estimates, so it fills all K slots (the hot item beats the heap minimum every time); (b) entries are never updated or removed when an item is already in the heap, so stale low estimates remain; (c) the sketch has no window: counts only grow, so "recent" is really all-time; (d) a sketch count is never decayed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a unit test with 3 items and heavy repetition, assert top() has distinct items; check the heap length versus distinct set.
  5. Root cause: The heap is keyed by (estimate, item) entries, not by item, so updates create duplicates.
  6. Fix:
cand = {}                                   # item -> latest estimate, size <= K
def on_event(item):
    cms.add(item)
    est = cms.est(item)
    if item in cand or len(cand) < K:
        cand[item] = est
    else:
        low = min(cand, key=cand.get)      # K is small; O(K) is fine
        if est > cand[low]:
            del cand[low]; cand[item] = est

Per window: one sketch per time bucket (60 one-minute buckets), summing the last 60 and dropping the oldest each minute. 7. Prevention: Property tests (distinct items, monotonic estimates), a replay test against exact counts, a window-expiry test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: For large K use an indexed heap with position map; do not keep re-sorting on every event.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Thread safety? -> Partition by item hash so one thread owns each item; no locks on the sketch.
  • Why not Space-Saving? -> It replaces the sketch-plus-heap pair with m counters and a guarantee; a good alternative.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "top pages" widget showed one URL ten times for a week; nobody noticed because it was still "the top".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Misses the duplicate-entry bug.
  • Hire: Fixes duplicates with a keyed candidate set.
  • Strong hire: Also notices no windowing, proposes bucketed sketches and tests.
